summary: Defines a metric for one-way packet loss across Internet paths. It was replaced by RFC 7680.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo defines how to measure how many packets are lost travelling one way across the Internet. It gives a single measurement worth zero or one, a way of taking many such measurements at random times, and a rule for reporting them so two systems get comparable numbers.

questions: how is packet loss measured in ippm
why use poisson sampling for network measurement
what counts as a lost packet
subtitle: A precise definition of what it means for a packet to be lost on a one-way Internet path, and how to sample and average it.

tldr.problem: Two measurement systems can disagree about packet loss unless they agree on what a lost packet is, how packets are spaced in time, and what is reported alongside the number.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a singleton metric whose value is zero or one, then a sample built by taking those singletons at times drawn from a Poisson process, then statistics over the sample. It also lists the four items that must be reported with a result.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2680 was a Proposed Standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7680.

today: RFC 2680 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 7680, which carries the same measurement definitions forward.

sections.title: Why One-way Loss and Not Round-trip Loss
sections.content:
The memo defines a metric for one-way packet loss across Internet paths, building on the IPPM Framework document. It is structured in three levels, and the separation between them matters: a singleton analytic metric called Type-P-One-way-Loss measures a single observation of packet transmission or loss; a sample, called Type-P-One-way-Loss-Poisson-Stream, measures a sequence of such singleton transmissions and losses taken at times from a Poisson process; and several statistics of the sample are defined on top of that.

Understanding one-way loss of Type-P packets from a source host to a destination host is useful for several reasons. Some applications do not perform well, or at all, if end-to-end loss between hosts is large relative to some threshold value. Excessive packet loss may make it difficult to support certain real-time applications. The larger the value of packet loss, the more difficult it is for transport-layer protocols to sustain high bandwidths. The sensitivity of real-time applications and of transport protocols to loss becomes especially important when very large delay-bandwidth products must be supported.

The memo gives four reasons for measuring one-way loss rather than round-trip loss. The path from a source to a destination may differ from the path back, so a round-trip measurement actually measures two distinct paths together. Even when the two paths are symmetric, they may have radically different performance characteristics because of asymmetric queueing. The performance of an application may depend mostly on the performance in one direction, for example a file transfer using TCP, which depends more on the direction the data flows than the direction the acknowledgements travel. And in quality-of-service enabled networks, provisioning in one direction may be radically different from the reverse, so the guarantees differ.
sections.plainLanguage: A round-trip number blends two journeys together. Measuring one direction at a time shows which way is going wrong and lets you check the guarantees in each direction separately.

sections.title: Four Clock Properties That Affect the Result
sections.content:
Whenever a time is mentioned in the memo, it is measured in seconds and fractions relative to UTC. Four distinct but related notions of clock uncertainty are described, each with the example the memo gives.

Synchronization measures the extent to which two clocks agree on what time it is. For example, the clock on one host might be 5.4 msec ahead of the clock on a second host. Accuracy measures the extent to which a given clock agrees with UTC. The clock on a host might be 27.1 msec behind UTC. Resolution measures the precision of a given clock. The clock on an old Unix host might advance only once every 10 msec, and thus have a resolution of only 10 msec. Skew measures the change of accuracy, or of synchronization, with time. A clock might gain 1.3 msec per hour and thus be 27.1 msec behind UTC at one time and only 25.8 msec an hour later.

The memo notes that these terms differ from those defined by the ITU-T documents, but that the differences derive from different backgrounds: the ITU-T documents have a telephony origin while the memo and the Framework have a computer systems background.
sections.plainLanguage: Any timing measurement depends on the clocks at both ends. Four properties of a clock matter: how well two clocks agree, how close one clock is to UTC, how finely it ticks, and how fast it drifts.

sections.title: The Single Measurement
sections.content:
The singleton metric is named Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss and takes three parameters: Src, the IP address of a host; Dst, the IP address of a host; and T, a time. Its value is either a zero, signifying successful transmission of the packet, or a one, signifying loss.

The definition is exact. A value of zero means that Src sent the first bit of a Type-P packet to Dst at wire-time T and that Dst received that packet. A value of one means that Src sent the first bit of a type-P packet to Dst at wire-time T and that Dst did not receive that packet. The metric is therefore zero exactly when the one-way delay is a finite value, and one exactly when the one-way delay is undefined.

The memo then works through the practical cases. A given methodology has to distinguish between a packet loss and a very large but finite delay; simple upper bounds, such as the 255 seconds theoretical upper bound on the lifetimes of IP packets, could be used. A packet that arrives corrupted is counted as lost. A packet duplicated along the path is counted as received, since multiple non-corrupt copies arriving at the destination still means the packet was not lost. A fragmented packet whose reassembly does not occur is deemed lost.
sections.plainLanguage: One measurement is a single yes-or-no: did the packet arrive? A corrupted packet counts as not arriving, and a duplicated one counts as arriving.

sections.title: Sampling at Times From a Poisson Process
sections.content:
The sample is named Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss-Poisson-Stream and takes five parameters: Src, Dst, a start time T0, a final time Tf, and an average rate lambda in reciprocal seconds. Its value is a sequence of pairs, each made of a time T and a loss value L that is either zero or one. The values of T in the sequence are monotonically increasing.

The definition is procedural. Given T0, Tf and lambda, a pseudo-random Poisson process beginning at or before T0, with average arrival rate lambda, and ending at or after Tf is computed. The time values greater than or equal to T0 and less than or equal to Tf are selected. At each of those times the singleton metric is evaluated. The value of the sample is the sequence of resulting time and loss pairs. If there are no such pairs, the sequence has length zero and the sample is said to be empty.

The memo does not constrain the value of lambda except to note the extremes: too large and the measurement traffic perturbs the network and itself causes congestion; too small and interesting network behaviour may not be captured. The Poisson process is used to avoid the effects of self-synchronization and to capture a sample that is as statistically unbiased as possible. It is also noted that loss rates observed by transport connections do not reflect unbiased samples, because TCP transmissions occur in bursts and because TCP adapts its transmission rate to minimise the loss it observes.
sections.plainLanguage: To get a series of measurements, the tester picks times at random intervals drawn from a mathematical pattern that avoids clumping, and takes one measurement at each of those times.

sections.title: Statistics of a Sample
sections.content:
Several statistics of the sample are offered, mostly to illustrate what could be done. The first is Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss-Average, the average of all the L values in the stream, which is undefined if the sample is empty.

The memo's worked example takes a sample with the results T1 0, T2 0, T3 1, T4 0, T5 0, and gives an average of 0.2.

It then notes the practical difficulty of measuring small loss rates. Since healthy Internet paths should be operating at loss rates below 1 percent, particularly if high delay-bandwidth products are to be sustained, the sample sizes needed might be larger than one would like. For example, if one wants to discriminate between various fractions of 1 percent over one-minute periods, then several hundred samples per minute might be needed, which would result in larger values of lambda than one would ordinarily want.

The memo adds a warning: although the loss threshold should be set so that errors in loss are not significant, if the possibility that a packet which arrived is counted as lost because the receiving instrument ran out of resources is significant compared with the loss rate of interest, the average will be meaningless.
sections.plainLanguage: The simplest statistic is the share of packets lost. Because good paths lose well under one percent of packets, measuring small differences takes hundreds of samples a minute.

sections.title: Security and Privacy of the Measurements
sections.content:
Conducting Internet measurements raises both security and privacy concerns. The memo does not specify an implementation of the metrics, so it does not directly affect the security of the Internet or of applications running on it, but implementations of these metrics must be mindful of both.

There are two kinds of harm. The measurements could cause harm because they are active and inject packets into the network. The measurement parameters must be carefully selected so that the measurements inject trivial amounts of additional traffic into the networks they measure. If they inject too much traffic they can skew the results of the measurement and, in extreme cases, cause congestion and denial of service.

The measurements themselves could be harmed by routers giving measurement traffic a different priority from normal traffic, or by an attacker injecting artificial measurement traffic. If routers can recognise measurement traffic and treat it separately, the measurements will not reflect actual user traffic. If an attacker injects artificial traffic that is accepted as legitimate, the loss rate will be artificially lowered. Measurement methodologies should therefore include techniques to reduce the probability that measurement traffic can be distinguished from normal traffic, and authentication techniques such as digital signatures may be used to guard against injected traffic attacks. The privacy concerns are limited by the fact that these measurements are active; unlike passive measurement, there can be no release of existing user data.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring the network means adding traffic to it, so the tester must keep the volume tiny. And because the traffic is visible to routers, someone could treat it specially or fake it.
